subject: chemistry
question_text: What are the differences between electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity?

verification.note: PREDICTED, not asked. This question comes from the enumeration sweep of the Classification chapter against the Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.53-55): the compare archetype between these two neighbouring properties is a standard board ask that the book skips — it defines both inside the trends LAQ but never asks them against each other. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+2 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. AI chemistry check 2026-08-25: both definitions and the three contrasts were re-checked against NCERT Class-11 and nothing marked was changed; the electron gain enthalpy why now records the sign convention (negative when energy is released, positive where the added electron must enter a filled or half-filled shell) so the card agrees with its sibling cards; one memory tip reworded to plain literal language. Status stays unverified. AI chemistry check 2026-08-25 (audit round 3): the first step's why called the noble gases 'the exception' with a positive electron gain enthalpy; beryllium, magnesium and nitrogen are positive too, and this chapter's ie1_ie2_factors and ie_nitrogen_oxygen cards teach that stability effect, so the why now names all of them. No marked line changed.

page_header: Classification of Elements – Periodic Properties · 4 marks

steps.label: Electron gain enthalpy
lines: Electron gain enthalpy: the enthalpy change
when an electron is added to an isolated
neutral gaseous atom.
It is a measurable energy, expressed in
kJ mol⁻¹.
steps.why: The comparison can only be marked if each property is first defined on its own; the equation pins electron gain enthalpy to a single free atom and a real energy change. For most elements energy is released, so the enthalpy change is negative. The value is positive wherever the added electron has to enter an already stable shell: the noble gases (filled ns²np⁶), beryllium and magnesium (filled ns²) and nitrogen (half-filled 2p³) all have positive electron gain enthalpies. The noble gases are the clearest case, not the only one.
common_mistakes: Defining it for an atom inside a molecule. It belongs to an isolated gaseous atom.
Leaving out the unit kJ mol⁻¹, which becomes one of the differences below.
steps.memory_tip: One free gas atom takes in one electron; the energy change of that event is the electron gain enthalpy.
steps.margin_note: Definition plus equation; the differences table below reuses both.

steps.label: Electronegativity
lines: Electronegativity: the ability of a bonded
atom to attract the shared pair of electrons
towards itself.
It is a relative number on a chosen scale
(fluorine = 4.0 on the Pauling scale) and has
no units.
steps.why: Electronegativity only exists inside a bond — there is no shared pair to attract in a free atom — and that single fact generates every difference listed below.
common_mistakes: Defining electronegativity for a free atom. It is a property of an atom in a molecule.
Giving electronegativity units. It is a pure number on a relative scale.
steps.memory_tip: No bond, no electronegativity: the property is defined only for an atom that is sharing a pair of electrons.
steps.margin_note: The Pauling value 4.0 for fluorine anchors the scale.

steps.label: The differences
lines: Differences:
1. Electron gain enthalpy belongs to an
isolated gaseous atom; electronegativity
belongs to a bonded atom in a molecule.
2. Electron gain enthalpy is a measured
energy in kJ mol⁻¹; electronegativity is a
relative number with no units.
3. Electron gain enthalpy has one value for
an element; electronegativity changes with
the oxidation state and the bonding
partner.

lines.text: Isolated atom, measured energy — bonded atom, relative number

steps.why: Each difference contrasts the same feature of both properties in one sentence — whose atom, what kind of quantity, how fixed — which is the pattern examiners can tick.
common_mistakes: Writing facts about each property separately instead of point-by-point contrasts.
Giving only one difference for the two marks. Two clear contrasts is the minimum.
steps.memory_tip: Contrast the same three features: whose atom, what quantity, how fixed.
steps.margin_note: Number the differences; each numbered contrast is tickable on its own.

insider_note: Half the marks are the differences, so plan it as two short definitions and then a numbered contrast list. Two point-against-point contrasts fill those two marks; two separate paragraphs about each property do not.
